title: The weight of empty space
subtitle: What you leave out is as deliberate — and as powerful — as what you put in.

principles.headline: Whitespace is not wasted space.
body: Every beginner designer's instinct is to fill. Every experienced designer's practice is to resist that instinct. White space is not the absence of design — it is design in its most confident form.
When you give elements room to breathe, you give users room to think. Crowded layouts create cognitive pressure. Spacious layouts create clarity. The emptiness is doing work you can't see.
principles.callout: A layout that feels 'empty' to the designer often feels 'calm' to the user.

principles.headline: Every element you add costs the user something.
body: Attention is finite. Every button, label, icon, and line of text is a micro-tax on the person using your product. The question isn't 'should we add this?' — it's 'is this worth what it costs?'
Most cluttered interfaces aren't the result of bad design. They're the result of too many stakeholders, too little restraint, and the mistaken belief that more information means more value.
principles.callout: The best interface element is the one you convinced someone not to add.

principles.headline: Reduction is a creative act.
body: It takes more skill to remove than to add. Anyone can put things on a page. It takes deep understanding of the problem — and the courage to be wrong — to take things away.
Editing is designing. The version with fewer elements is usually the version that required more design thinking, not less.
principles.callout: Simplicity is not the absence of complexity. It's complexity that has been fully understood and then resolved.

actions.title: Before adding anything to a design, ask: what can I remove first?
actions.desc: Make subtraction your default move. Start each design session by looking for what doesn't belong.
actions.example: "I had seven items in the nav. I asked myself which three the user actually needs on their first visit. Now there are four."

actions.title: In your next critique, present the version with the most removed.
actions.desc: Don't show the 'safe' version with everything in. Show the stripped-back version and let the room argue for what to add back.
actions.example: "I showed the team a version with no secondary actions at all. They had to justify every one they wanted to restore."

actions.title: Pick one UI element in your current work and spend 10 minutes trying to eliminate it.
actions.desc: If you can't eliminate it, the exercise still sharpens your understanding of why it belongs.
actions.example: "I spent 10 minutes trying to remove the breadcrumb. I couldn't. But now I understand exactly why it's there — which made me redesign it better."

actions.title: Design a version that's half the visual weight of your current design.
actions.desc: Cut font sizes, reduce contrast levels, shrink UI elements. Then bring them back only where they earn their presence.
actions.example: "I made everything 20% smaller and 20% lighter. The thing that looked worst was the primary CTA — which told me it wasn't doing its job in the original."

actions.title: When defending a decision to remove something, lead with user cost, not aesthetic preference.
actions.desc: 'It looks cleaner' loses arguments. 'It reduces the time to the primary action by removing a competing choice' wins them.
actions.example: "I didn't say it 'felt busy'. I said 'users are spending 4 seconds looking at this section before making a decision. If we remove it, that decision becomes faster.'"

actions.title: At end of week, look at something you shipped and ask: what's the one thing I'd remove now?
actions.desc: Design is never done. The edit that wasn't possible before shipping is still worth noting.
actions.example: "I shipped it with the helper text. Three weeks later I can see it's unnecessary — users never read it and the input is clear enough without it."

coda.quote: The most powerful design tool you have is the delete key.
coda.footer: Restraint is not timidity. It is the highest form of design confidence.

closingQuote.text: It seems that perfection is attained not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing more to remove.
